claim: Three monobodies (Xph15, Xph18, and Xph20) were selected and isolated that bind to the tandem PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: We have recently selected and isolated 10FN3-derived clones that bind to the tandem PDZ domains of PSD-95 (Rimbault et al., 2019; Figure 1a). Three of the evolved 10FN3 domains, which displayed specific recognition of the target, were characterized in depth in particular with respect to the identification of their respective epitope.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Rimbault et al., 2019) and reference to Figure 1a showing the binding models.

claim: Xph15 and Xph20 share a similar epitope situated on PDZ domain 1 on the opposite side of the surface compared to the canonical functional region of the domain.
source: Two monobodies (Xph15 and Xph20) shared a similar epitope situated on PDZ domain 1 on the opposite side of the surface compared to the canonical functional region of the domain.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the epitope locations of the monobodies.

claim: Xph18 presents an extended epitope that spreads on both PDZ domains 1 and 2, in regions distant from the two binding grooves.
source: The third monobody (Xph18) presented an extended epitope that spread on both domains 1 and 2, also in regions distant from the two binding grooves.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the epitope of Xph18.

claim: The three evolved binders do not directly block the two PDZ domain-binding sites.
source: As the three evolved binders did not directly block the two PDZ domain-binding sites, we envisaged their use as minimally interfering targeting modules.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a conclusion from the epitope characterization.

claim: NMR titration experiments showed that a stargazin-derived peptide can fully interact with both PDZ1 and PDZ2 in the presence of Xph15, Xph18, or Xph20.
source: A peptide derived from the C-terminus of a known PSD-95 PDZ domain binder, the auxiliary AMPA receptor (AMPAR) subunit stargazin (Stg), was titrated against a 15N-labeled PSD-95 tandem construct containing PDZ domains 1 and 2. In addition, the peptide was titrated against the same 15N-labeled PSD-95 construct pre-bound with either Xph15, Xph18, or Xph20. A series of 2D 15N-HSQC spectra were used to follow PSD-95 residues during each titration, and in all cases residues on both PDZ1 and PDZ2 were able to fully interact with the Stg peptide.
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The PDZ domain-binding properties are not detectably modified in the presence of the evolved Xph binders.
source: Qualitatively, each of the reporter residues shown in Figure 1b has similar titration behavior and final crosspeak positions in the 15N-HSQC spectra, and therefore supports the fact that the peptide binding is generally unaffected by the presence of the binders.
evidence: The claim is supported by qualitative analysis of NMR data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The presence of Xph18 impaired binding of a fluorescent divalent stargazin-derived probe in fluorescence polarization assays.
source: Competitions performed in the absence of ligand or with a naïve clone (Xph0 that does not bind PSD-95) (Rimbault et al., 2019) were similar to the ones obtained with Xph15 and 20. In contrast, the presence of Xph18 impaired binding of the fluorescent divalent probe.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The inhibitory effect of Xph18 on divalent ligand binding was abolished by the use of monovalent stargazin-derived probe and competitor.
source: This effect was abolished, in agreement with the NMR observations, by the use of monovalent stargazin-derived probe and competitor (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The inhibitory effect of Xph18 results from conformational constraints imposed on the two domains orientation rather than from blocking or direct impairment of the PDZ domain-binding ability.
source: These results suggest that the observed inhibitory effect results from the conformational constraints imposed on the two domains orientation by Xph18 binding rather than from the blocking or direct impairment of the PDZ domain-binding ability.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental results from fluorescence polarization and NMR experiments.

claim: FRET/FLIM assays in cell lines showed no significant effect on the measured donor lifetime associated with the binding of Xph15, Xph18, or Xph20 to full-length PSD-95 in the presence of stargazin.
source: We therefore evaluated by a FRET/FLIM assay in cell lines the binding of PSD-95 to its partners (represented here by stargazin) via its PDZ domains in the presence and absence of the monobodies. We used both the recombinant full-length proteins (Figure 1e) as well as a reporter system that focused on interactions mediated by PDZ domains 1 and 2 (Figure 1f). In both cases, even at high molar ratio, we could not detect any significant effect on the measured donor lifetime associated with the binding of either Xph15, Xph18, or Xph20.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRET/FLIM data shown in Figure 1e and 1f.

claim: Expression of Xph15, Xph18, or Xph20 does not affect AMPAR-mediated synaptic currents in mouse hippocampal neurons.
source: Comparison of control eGFP-infected mouse neurons to neurons infected with Xph15, Xph18, or Xph20 did not reveal any significant difference on spontaneous mEPSCs (Figure 2a–e). The mean amplitude values were not modified by the presence of any of the PSD-95 binders (Figure 2b, control: 21.3 ± 2.1 pA [n = 19]; Xph15: 24.9 ± 3.9 pA [n = 15]; Xph18: 21.3 ± 2.0 pA [n = 17]; Xph20: 18.0 ± 2.2 pA [n = 16]; mean ± SEM with p>0.4 for the three clones using nonparametric Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Dunn's post hoc test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2a-e.

claim: Expression of the three monobodies does not affect the lateral mobility of surface AMPARs.
source: In agreement with the absence of modification of excitatory currents, no detectable effect was observed for Xph-expressing neurons vs control non-transfected ones on the lateral mobility of surface AMPARs. The distributions of diffusion coefficients were highly similar for all conditions (Figure 2g, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). Importantly, the percentage of mobile AMPARs was not increased in the presence of any of the clones as could have been expected from a binder that would have perturbed interactions with either of the first two PDZ domains (Figure 2h, control: 34.9 ± 9.5% [n = 26]; Xph15: 36.9 ± 11.9% [n = 27]; Xph18: 34.6 ± 9.9% [n = 18]; Xph20: 32.2 ± 10.5% [n = 7]; mean ± SD with p>0.73 by ordinary one-way ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-particle tracking data shown in Figure 2f-h.

claim: The PSD-95 interactome appears unaffected by Xph20-eGFP expression as determined by mass spectrometry.
source: When comparing the two conditions, eGFP or Xph20-eGFP expression (Figure 2i), the abundance of most identified proteins was globally unaffected (abundance ratio close to 1 and/or low statistical significance with p-values above 0.05). All known PSD-95 partners that were identified in the two independent experiments (~40 identified partners per experiment) fell in that category.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Xph15, Xph18, and Xph20 fused to eGFP show strong enrichment on dendrites at postsynapse-like structures with a mean intensity enrichment ratio around 7 compared to the rest of the dendrite.
source: For all the binders tested, the eGFP signal was similarly strongly enriched on dendrites at postsynapse-like structures. The objects we observed presented in all cases a mean intensity enrichment ratio compared to the rest of the dendrite around 7 (Figure 3b; PSD95.FingR: 6.4 ± 3.0; Xph15: 6.4 ± 1.4; Xph18: 7.4 ± 2.1; Xph20: 8.4 ± 2.1; mean ± SD with p>0.72 by ordinary one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's multiple-comparison tests).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a-b.

claim: The colocalization values obtained for the three Xph clones with PSD-95 immunostaining were significantly higher than for PSD95.FingR.
source: The colocalization of PSD-95-positive objects detected by antibody immunostaining with the puncta revealed by the four investigated probes was overall strong (Figure 3d, PSD95.FingR: 75.4 ± 30.9; Xph15: 98.4 ± 4.8; Xph18: 95.5 ± 11.1; Xph20: 95.2 ± 13.4; mean ± SD with p<0.0001 for PSD95.FingR vs the other binders by ordinary one-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett's multiple-comparison test), in agreement with reported values for PSD-95.FingR (Cook et al., 2019; Gross et al., 2013). Remarkably, the values obtained for the three Xph clones were significantly higher than for PSD95.FingR.
evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 3c-d.

claim: The three monobodies showed fast exchange rates and high mobile fractions (75%, 71%, and 76% for Xph15, Xph18, and Xph20, respectively) in FRAP experiments.
source: As expected, on the minute timescale, the three monobodies showed fast exchange rates (Supplementary file 1) as well as high mobile fractions (Figure 3f and Supplementary file 1; 75, 71, and 76% for Xph15, Xph18, and Xph20, respectively) compared to the values reported in basal conditions for PSD-95-GFP knock-in (~10% after 60 min [Fortin et al., 2014]) or to the values obtained here with a transfected PSD-95-eGFP (37%).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 3e-g and Supplementary file 1.

claim: PSD-95 knock-down with shRNA led to a clear and consistent loss of signal for both Xph15 and Xph20 intrabodies and the corresponding antibody labeling.
source: While the conditions with the scramble shRNA led to a labeling very similar to what was obtained previously in its absence, the use of the shRNA against PSD-95 was associated with a clear and consistent loss of signal, in particular no detectable puncta, both for the two Xph intrabodies and the corresponding antibody labeling (Figure 4a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by knock-down experiment data shown in Figure 4a-c.

claim: Strong correlation was observed between Xph15-eGFP or Xph20-eGFP and PSD-95-mScarlet-I, with Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.84 and 0.87 for Xph15 and Xph20, respectively.
source: Systematic analysis of the two fluorescence signals (eGFP and mScarlet-I) indicated strong correlation, with Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.84 and 0.87 for Xph15 (Figure 4e) and Xph20 (Figure 4f), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4d-f.

claim: Xph15-mNeonGreen probe showed about 70% fluorescence recovery in less than 15 minutes after STED photobleaching.
source: About 70% of the initial fluorescence was recovered in less than 15 min (Figure 5d), allowing the area to be efficiently imaged repetitively.
evidence: The claim is supported by STED recovery data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Xph15-SNAP-tag labeled with BG-SiR allowed timelapse STED acquisitions at about a 1 min (50 s) frequency with minimal impact on the STED signal.
source: Photostability and dynamic exchange of the probe allowed to perform timelapse acquisitions at about a 1 min (50 s) frequency with minimal impact on the STED signal (Figure 5g), thereby illustrating the advantage of organic dyes over fluorescent proteins for such applications.
evidence: The claim is supported by STED timelapse data shown in Figure 5g.

claim: PALM analysis of Xph20-mEos3.2 in fixed neurons revealed a non-homogeneous distribution with the presence of higher density clusters representing about half the number of detections measured for the whole synaptic objects.
source: Further analysis of the synaptic objects using the Tesselation-based segmentation method (Levet et al., 2015) revealed a non-homogeneous distribution with the presence of higher density clusters. The clusters represented about half the number of detections measured for the whole synaptic objects.
evidence: The claim is supported by PALM data analysis shown in Figure 6c-d.

claim: Estimation of single-emitter contribution suggests the presence of ~200–300 probe copies per synaptic objects, consistent with reported estimations of PSD-95 synaptic copies.
source: A tentative estimation of single-emitter contribution (Figure 6d, Figure 6—figure supplement 1e, median ~10 detections) suggests the presence of ~200–300 probe copies per synaptic objects. This value is consistent with reported estimations of PSD-95 synaptic copies (Chen et al., 2005; Sugiyama et al., 2005) and therefore suggests a close to stoichiometric labeling of the endogenous protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by PALM data analysis shown in Figure 6d and Figure 6—figure supplement 1e, and comparison with literature values.

claim: Morphological analysis of PALM objects and clusters provided dimensions consistent with previous reports for PSD-95-mEos2 fusions with PALM or by STORM by labeling endogenous PSD-95 with antibodies.
source: Morphological analysis of the objects and clusters provided dimensions consistent with previous reports for PSD-95-mEos2 fusions with PALM (Nair et al., 2013) or by STORM by labeling endogenous PSD-95 with antibodies (Compans et al., 2019) (length: 434.5 ± 39.9 and 178.0 ± 39.3 nm; width: 251.1 ± 39.2 and 99.1 ± 22.4 nm for the objects and clusters, respectively, Figure 6e).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 6e and comparison with literature values.

claim: Single-particle tracking PALM of Xph20-mEos3.2 in live neurons showed ~80% of particles confined or immobile and only ~20% mobile.
source: The probe diffusion coefficient showed a Gaussian-like distribution, which suggests a homogeneous population, with ~80% of particles confined or immobile and only ~20% mobile (Figure 6i).
evidence: The claim is supported by spt-PALM data shown in Figure 6i.

claim: Single-particle-tracking-PALM measurements could be repeated over the course of 30 min without detectable differences in the diffusion distribution.
source: Importantly, single-particle-tracking-PALM measurements could be repeated over the course of 30 min without detectable differences in the diffusion distribution (Figure 6j), demonstrating that the method is robust and compatible with hour timescale live investigations such as needed for synaptic plasticity events.
evidence: The claim is supported by spt-PALM time course data shown in Figure 6j.

claim: Xph20-SNAP-tag fusion allowed efficient labeling for DNA-PAINT with a clear synaptic enrichment comparable to other validated fusions.
source: In contrast, and consistently with the STED experiments, the SNAP-tag fusion allowed an efficient labeling with a clear synaptic enrichment comparable to the ones obtained with the other validated fusions (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-PAINT data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Xph15-GCaMP6f showed a clear synaptic enrichment in comparison to the original sensor expressed alone.
source: A first attempt with GCaMP6f (Chen et al., 2013) as simple fusion to Xph15 expressed in rat primary culture neurons clearly indicated the feasibility of the approach (Figure 8—figure supplement 1a and b, Figure 8—videos 1 and 2). Indeed, even in the absence of the regulation system, a clear synaptic enrichment of the engineered calcium reporter was observed in comparison to the original sensor expressed alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1a-b.

claim: The expression regulation system was necessary to allow a clear synaptic enrichment of Xph20-GCaMP7f when using the CAG promoter.
source: Expression levels of the reporter were higher with the CAG promoter both in the absence and presence of the regulation system. However, in this case, the latter was necessary to allow a clear synaptic enrichment of GCaMP7f (Figure 8b–d) as its absence, combined with higher expression levels, led to a homogeneous distribution of the calcium reporter in the dendrite (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8b-d and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Xph15 and Xph20 constitute robust and valuable modules to engineer super-resolution imaging probes for endogenous PSD-95.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that Xph15 and Xph20 constitute robust and valuable modules to engineer SRI probes for endogenous PSD-95. Indeed, by adapting the recognition and the reporting modules together with the use of a system for regulation of the probe production, we show that they can be easily exploited to provide a straightforward access to both the nanoscale mapping and the dynamics of this key synaptic protein.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the various super-resolution imaging experiments presented.

claim: Overexpression of fluorescent protein-fused PSD-95 leads to an increase in dendritic spine number and size, as well as frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) and affects synaptic plasticity.
source: In particular, overexpression of fluorescent protein-fused PSD-95 for imaging purposes is phenotypically marked and leads to an increase in dendritic spine number and size, as well as frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) and affects synaptic plasticity (El-Husseini et al., 2000; Nikonenko et al., 2008; Zhang and Lisman, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PSD-95 plays a key role in organizing receptors, ion channels, adhesion proteins, enzymes, and cytoskeletal proteins at excitatory synapses.
source: PSD-95 plays a key role in organizing receptors, ion channels, adhesion proteins, enzymes, and cytoskeletal proteins at excitatory synapses (Won et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Up- or downregulation of PSD-95 results in critical alterations in synapse morphology and function.
source: As a consequence, up- or downregulation of PSD-95 results in critical alterations in synapse morphology and function (Won et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PSD95.FingR can recognize SAP97 and SAP102, two closely related proteins to PSD-95.
source: However, in both cases, the precise epitopes remain non-characterized, and, furthermore, one of the binders, PSD95.FingR, can also recognize SAP97 and SAP102, two closely related proteins (Gross et al., 2013; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The three monobodies (Xph15, Xph18, Xph20) recognized epitopes situated outside of the PDZ domain-binding groove in regions not subjected to post-translational modifications.
source: Importantly, all the clones recognized epitopes situated outside of the PDZ domain-binding groove in regions not subjected to post-translational modifications.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the properties of the monobodies.

claim: The epitopes recognized by Xph15, Xph18, and Xph20 are conserved in a number of species (e.g., rodents, human, etc.).
source: Importantly, these epitopes are conserved in a number of species (e.g., rodents, human, etc.) and are not subject to post-translational modifications.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the properties of the epitopes.

claim: The 10FN3 scaffold is devoid of internal disulfide bonds, alleviating the risk of susceptibility to the intracellular reducing environment.
source: Furthermore, we note that in the context of intrabody-like approaches, the 10FN3 scaffold, from which the binders are derived, is devoid of internal disulfide bonds, typically found, for instance, in antibody fragments, and thereby alleviating the risk of susceptibility to the intracellular reducing environment.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the properties of the 10FN3 scaffold.

claim: The regulation system is efficient if the targeted protein is not nuclear and the affinity of the evolved binder for the target is superior to the one of the appended zinc finger for its binding motif.
source: In other words, the system is efficient if, on the one hand, the targeted protein is not nuclear and, on the other hand, the affinity of the evolved binder for the target is superior to the one of the appended zinc finger for its binding motif incorporated into the expression plasmid.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the regulation system.

claim: The regulation system was functional for evolved binding modules with affinities in the 1–0.1 µM range in combination with a highly expressed target such as PSD-95.
source: We have observed here that the regulation system was functional for evolved binding modules with affinities in the 1–0.1 µM range in combination with a highly expressed target such as PSD-95.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the regulation system performance.

claim: The specific use of mScarlet-I and HaloTag resulted in the failure of the regulation system.
source: We note, however, that while most of the reporter cargos we tried were compatible with this approach, the specific use of mScarlet-I and HaloTag resulted in the failure of the regulation system for reasons that are still unclear.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing limitations of the regulation system.

claim: Xph15 and Xph20 constitute the only genetically encoded systems that allow the strict specific detection of endogenous PSD-95 for live and advanced imaging applications.
source: Indeed, Xph15- and Xph20-derived probes currently constitute the only genetically encoded systems that allow the strict specific detection of endogenous PSD-95 for live and advanced imaging applications with, in addition, a comprehensive description of their target binding properties (epitopes, affinities and kinetics, absence detectable interference, etc.).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text comparing the tools to existing probes.

claim: The binding of Xph clones and PDZ domain ligands are independent events that are not detectably affected by long-range conformational modifications.
source: Together, the NMR study and the fluorescence polarization assay indicate that the binding of, on the one hand, Xph clones and, on the other hand, PDZ domain ligands are independent events that are not detectably affected by long-range conformational modifications.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion from NMR and fluorescence polarization experiments.

claim: Due to the constraints imposed by Xph18 binding on the conformational flexibility of the two PDZ domains, certain complex interactions may be impaired.
source: However, we note that due to the constraints imposed by Xph18 binding on the conformational flexibility of the two PDZ domains, certain complex interactions may be impaired.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a caveat regarding Xph18.

claim: The binding of neither Xph15, Xph18, nor Xph20 affects endogenous PSD-95 function in its native environment as judged by the absence of impact on AMPAR properties and conservation of its interactome.
source: Altogether, these experiments indicate that the binding of neither Xph15, Xph18, nor Xph20 affects endogenous PSD-95 function in its native environment as judged by the absence of impact on AMPAR properties and conservation of its interactome.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion from multiple functional assays.

claim: The three monobodies comply with the criterion of not detectably affecting PSD-95 function, albeit with some reservation for Xph18.
source: The absence of any detectable effect of Xph clone binding on PSD-95 function constituted an obligatory first criterion to consider their use as a non-interfering imaging probe. As the three monobodies comply with this criterion (albeit with some reservation for Xph18), we next focused on confirming their capacity to label endogenous PSD-95 and on evaluating their specific properties as fluorescent probes.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a conclusion from functional assays.

claim: The three monobodies label PSD-95 efficiently as demonstrated by strong overlap of the GFP signal with the immunostaining of endogenous PSD-95.
source: Considering the generally strong overlap of the GFP signal with the immunostaining of endogenous PSD-95, we conclude that the three monobodies label PSD-95 efficiently.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion from immunostaining colocalization experiments.

claim: The difference in colocalization between Xph clones and PSD95.FingR is interpreted as a direct benefit from the specificity of the Xph clones for PSD-95 while PSD95.FingR may also report the presence of SAP97 and SAP102 paralogs.
source: We interpret this difference as a direct benefit from the specificity of the Xph clones for PSD-95 while PSD95.FingR, which can also bind SAP97 and SAP102, may also report to some extent the presence of these two paralog proteins.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the colocalization data.

claim: The expression regulation system applied to the Xph binders allows for long expression schemes without excessive or detectable over-production of the probe.
source: In particular, as reported for PSD95.FingR, the expression regulation system applied to the Xph binders allows for long expression schemes without excessive or detectable over-production of the probe.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the regulation system.

claim: The measured mobile fractions and half-lives from FRAP experiments are consistent with the SPR kinetics measurements.
source: The measured mobile fractions and the half-lives (~16, 71, and 70 s for Xph15, Xph18, and Xph20, respectively) are consistent with the SPR kinetics measurements, with Xph15 being the fastest and Xph18 the slowest.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text comparing FRAP and SPR data.

claim: The Xph-derived probes exchange and are being renewed at a faster rate than their target PSD-95.
source: We note that the results we obtained here for the probes account for the behavior of both the free and the PSD-95-bound populations. However, considering the large difference between the values obtained for the probes and for PSD-95, we can reasonably conclude that the Xph-derived probes exchange and are being renewed at a faster rate than their target.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion from FRAP data analysis.

claim: Xph15 and Xph20 specifically recognize endogenous PSD-95 in its native environment as demonstrated by knock-down experiments.
source: PSD-95 knock-down effect manifested itself by an eGFP fluorescence signal almost exclusively nuclear indicating the absence of cytosolic target for intrabodies (Figure 4a) and was quantitatively observed both in detected objects (Figure 4b) and over entire dendritic segments (Figure 4c) demonstrating the specific recognition of endogenous PSD-95 by Xph15 and Xph20.
evidence: The claim is supported by knock-down experiment data shown in Figure 4a-c.

claim: Xph20 should be preferred for most applications as the tightest binder, but the faster binding kinetics of Xph15 can be exploited to favor rapid renewal of the probes in live conditions.
source: Despite the differences in affinities and binding kinetics of Xph15 and Xph20, both allowed an efficient and specific labeling of PSD-95 independently of the associated reporter group (eGFP, mNeonGreen, SNAP-tag, mEos3.2, GCaMP). Xph20, as the tightest binder, should therefore be preferred for most applications. However, the faster binding kinetics of Xph15 can also be exploited to favor rapid renewal of the probes in live conditions, a decisive advantage when photobleaching prevents time-based experiments.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the characterized properties of the binders.

claim: The fast-exchanging properties of the probes could be an advantage for STED imaging by allowing fast renewal of the probes and repeated acquisitions of the same region.
source: A major drawback of STED is the high illumination intensities required in particular for efficient depletion that often results in photobleaching of the fluorophore. In this context, the fast-exchanging properties of the probes could be an advantage and allow, by fast renewal of the probes, repeated acquisitions of the same region.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the properties of the probes.

claim: Xph20-mEos3.2 provides an accurate snapshot of PSD-95 nanoscale distribution in fixed samples.
source: Together, these results indicate that Xph20-mEos3.2 provides an accurate snapshot of PSD-95 nanoscale distribution in fixed samples.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion from PALM data analysis.

claim: In spt-PALM conditions, the probe is essentially detecting probes bound to PSD-95 rather than freely diffusive unbound probes.
source: These results are highly similar to those obtained with a mEos2-fused (Chazeau et al., 2014) or a mVenus-fused PSD-95 (Fortin et al., 2014), suggesting that, in these conditions, we are essentially detecting probes bound to PSD-95. Indeed, a freely diffusive emitter, such as an unbound probe, would be characterized by faster diffusion coefficients (Chazeau et al., 2014) that could not be detected in these experimental conditions.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of spt-PALM data based on comparison with literature.

claim: Both the Xph15 and Xph20 binding modules can be exploited to target gene-encoded modules other than fluorescent proteins to excitatory synapses.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that both the Xph15 and Xph20 binding modules can also be exploited to target gene-encoded module other than fluorescent proteins to excitatory synapses.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion from GCaMP targeting experiments.

claim: The probes will open up numerous possibilities for investigations against various neuronal targets by providing straightforward solutions for the monitoring of PSD-95 in the context of multi-proteins studies.
source: Importantly, given the central role of PSD-95 in synaptic function, we anticipate that the probes will open up numerous possibilities for investigations against various neuronal targets by providing straightforward solutions for the monitoring of PSD-95 in the context of multi-proteins studies.
evidence: The claim is a prediction about future applications of the probes.

claim: A multiplexed ReMoRA approach to label the PSD-95 paralogs would open numerous possibilities for investigating the respective role of each of these major neuronal actors.
source: A multiplexed ReMoRA approach to label the PSD-95 paralogs would open numerous possibilities for investigating the respective role of each of these major neuronal actors notably by providing access to advance imaging approaches with minimal interference on the targeted endogenous proteins.
evidence: The claim is a prediction about future applications of the approach.
